definition: A promise by a third party (here usually NVIDIA or Google) to buy, or pay for, data-center capacity that the operator fails to sell to customers. It lowers the operator's financing risk and borrowing cost.
When a supplier lends to, invests in or guarantees its own customers so they can buy its products. Common in telecom equipment around 1999–2001, where it amplified the bust.
Revenue a company has under signed contract but not yet delivered (often called remaining performance obligations). It shows demand visibility, not cash: contracts can be delayed or renegotiated.
A contract in which the buyer pays for reserved capacity whether or not it uses it. Neoclouds sign multi-year take-or-pay deals with AI labs and hyperscalers and then borrow against them.

Debt secured by a fleet of GPUs and the customer contracts that rent them out, often drawn in stages as hardware is delivered (a delayed-draw term loan). The lender's risk depends on contract quality and GPU resale value.
A long-term commitment by a large buyer (for example Microsoft or Meta) to rent a provider's future capacity. It lets the provider raise capital before the data center is built.
The open-source batch scheduler that queues and places jobs on most supercomputers and many AI training clusters. Its developer SchedMD was acquired by NVIDIA in December 2025.
The open-source system that runs containerised software across a cluster of machines; the default control plane of cloud computing. Add-ons such as Kueue and KAI Scheduler teach it to share GPUs.
Starting all parts of a distributed job at the same time or not at all, so that 1,000 GPUs do not sit idle waiting for the 1,001st. Schedulers such as Slurm, Kueue and KAI Scheduler support it.
The Kubernetes GPU scheduler from Run:ai that NVIDIA open-sourced in 2025 (Apache 2.0); it handles GPU sharing, queues, fairness and topology-aware placement.
An Israeli GPU-orchestration software company NVIDIA bought in 2024 (about $700M reported); its platform pools GPUs across teams and was fully open-sourced in October 2026.
NVIDIA's operations software for AI factories (launched 2025): cluster provisioning, Run:ai and Slurm scheduling, health monitoring and automatic job and hardware recovery.
An open, modular software portfolio for running multi-tenant AI factories that NVIDIA introduced in 2026, bundling KAI Scheduler, Run:ai, Cloud Functions, Grove and Dynamo among others.

NVIDIA's own GPU cloud service (2023), hosted inside Oracle, Microsoft, Google and AWS data centers on capacity NVIDIA rents. Most of it was reportedly redirected to NVIDIA's internal research in 2025.
An NVIDIA marketplace (2025) that routes developers to GPU capacity owned by partner clouds such as CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius and Crusoe; NVIDIA does not own the hardware.

A platform that lists GPU capacity from many providers and lets buyers rent it by the hour or week (for example Vast.ai, SF Compute or NVIDIA's Lepton). It competes on price and flexibility rather than service.
Contracted power is data-center capacity (in MW or GW) a cloud has signed for; active power is what is energised and billing today. The gap is build-out still to be financed and delivered.
A profit recorded because an investment's market or appraised value rose, without selling it. It lifts reported earnings but is not cash and reverses if prices fall.
A stake in a private company (for example OpenAI or Anthropic) with no quoted price; it is carried at cost and adjusted when new funding rounds reveal a different price.
The non-hyperscale half of NVIDIA's Data Center revenue since Q1 FY2027: AI clouds and neoclouds, sovereign projects, industrial and enterprise buyers.
AI infrastructure built or funded by a nation (or for it) so that data, models and compute stay under national control; often delivered through local neoclouds or telecom operators.
